demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'I have no future' is a broad, severe hopelessness appraisal, while 'others can see what happened to me just by looking at me' implies a visible stigma/marked external sign. For a trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, the latter is hard to justify clinically unless there is disfigurement or public exposure, neither of which is represented elsewhere.

issues.item: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: For a male delivery driver whose trauma was accidentally causing serious injury to another person, the appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him by looking at him is hard to reconcile with the trauma type unless there are visible injuries or marked stigma, which are not otherwise represented. The other selected appraisals centre on guilt and responsibility, so this item pulls toward a different formulation theme and is not well aligned with the otherwise coherent guilt-based negative appraisal pattern.

vignette:
Ravi Patel, a 34-year-old married delivery driver, came to treatment after months of carrying the same scene in his mind with a kind of punishing clarity. On an ordinary afternoon run, while backing his van out of a tight loading area, he struck a pedestrian he had not seen in his blind spot, and the person fell hard enough to require emergency care. Ravi had not meant to harm anyone, but from the moment he got out and saw the person on the ground, blood at the temple and strangers yelling for help, he experienced the event not as an accident but as a failure of character. He kept returning to the thought that he should have protected others and failed, that he ought to have done more to stop what happened, and that the injury happened because of the way he acted.

In the weeks that followed, Ravi replayed the moment from the driver’s seat over and over, measuring himself against what he thought he should have seen or done. He became convinced that if he had checked more carefully, if he had moved more slowly, if he had been a better man in that split second, the other person would not have been hurt. He spoke in absolutes about the guilt, saying he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. The fact that he was only trying to do his job did little to soften this belief; to him, the outcome proved that his own carelessness and hesitation were the cause. He had once taken pride in being dependable, the person who arrived on time and kept things moving for his family, but now that same responsibility felt corrupted, as if every delivery required him to carry the knowledge that one mistake could injure someone badly.

That interpretation began to shape how he moved through his days. Ravi grew wary of the warehouse lot, the narrow alleys behind apartment blocks, and any street where pedestrians could step out without warning, because each one seemed capable of recreating the same disaster. At work, he drove more stiffly and with constant self-monitoring, scanning mirrors and corners with a tense vigilance that left him exhausted by midday. He avoided speaking about the accident with his wife, partly because he did not want to burden her, and partly because he feared that saying it aloud would make the truth more permanent: that he had failed to protect another person and could not undo it. Over time, the shame widened into his home life as well, where he sat through dinner with his mind elsewhere, distracted by the conviction that he had proven himself unsafe and unworthy.

The more Ravi judged himself, the less room there was for anything except the injury and his responsibility for it. He found himself tracing every detail of that afternoon—the angle of the van, the noise from the dock, the moment he turned—looking for the exact point where a better person would have acted differently. Even now, months later, he describes the memory as something he cannot put down: the injured man’s body on the pavement, the panic in bystanders’ voices, and the immediate certainty that he should have protected others and did not. That certainty has become the lens through which he sees not only the accident but his entire life, and it is what brings him to therapy now. What he hopes for is relief from a guilt that has begun to govern his work, his marriage, and his sense of himself; what he fears most is that he will spend the rest of his life unable to forgive the person he believes caused it.
